chunks: How steppers hold position. The question: How do stepper motors hold a certain position?
A stepper holds its position by magnetism.
When you keep a steady current flowing in the right coils, the rotor (the turning part) settles into the spot where it lines up with the magnetic field.
If something pushes it away, a magnetic pull brings it back. No sensor or feedback is involved. The cost is that the current must keep flowing, which makes heat.
Picture a marble resting at the bottom of a shallow bowl. Nudge it and it rolls back to the middle, and the harder you push, the stronger the pull back, up to a point.
Push it over the rim and it drops into the next bowl along. The coils make the bowl, and the "holding torque" is how steep the bowl gets before the rim.
The analogy breaks in one place: switch the current off and the bowl nearly vanishes.
Near zero the torque is a straight spring line with stiffness 22. 5 N·m/rad. It bends over and peaks at ±1. 8° (one full step, 90° electrical) at the holding torque.
Beyond that the torque falls and reaches zero at 3. 6° (the red dashed line, unstable); push further and the torque reverses and drags the shaft to the next equilibrium 7.
2° away. The black marker shows the deflection for a 0. 2 N·m static load; the orange dashed lines mark the ±1. 8° torque peaks.
Holding torque: the largest twist the energized motor resists without slipping. Restoring torque: the pull back toward the resting spot when the shaft is pushed away.
Detent torque: the weak holding left when the power is off. Lost step: the rotor jumps to a different resting spot after an overload, and the controller does not know.
Hold current: the current kept in the coils while the motor is stationary.
Take a motor with 0. 45 N·m of holding torque. A load of 0. 225 N·m, half the limit, pushes the shaft only about 0. 6 degrees off its spot, and it stays there.
Raise the load above 0. 45 N·m and the shaft slips by 7. 2 degrees, or a multiple of it. Meanwhile, holding at 1. 7 amps through its two 1. 5 ohm coils burns about 8.
7 watts with no mechanical work. Halving the current cuts the heat to a quarter but also roughly halves the holding torque. That is the whole idea.
"A stepper holds position by magnetic alignment.

With the right coils energised with steady current, the rotor sits in a stable equilibrium, and any displacement creates a restoring torque like a spring, roughly T h sine (N r change in theta) , so no feedback is needed.
Holding torque is the peak of that restoring torque; beyond it the rotor slips by whole electrical cycles.
The cost is continuous current and heat; reducing the current reduces holding torque in proportion. With power off only the small detent torque remains."
